sections.figure_alt: A shaded elliptical disk centered in the plane.
sections.body_md:
A positive definite matrix already draws ellipses as level sets of a quadratic form. This problem uses the other picture. Apply a symmetric positive definite matrix \(B\) to the unit disk, then translate by a center \(d\). The image is an elliptical disk. Its area is proportional to \(\det B\).

A polytope is an intersection of half-spaces. The ellipsoid sits inside when it sits in every half-space. On the unit disk, a linear function peaks at a value equal to the length of its coefficient vector, so the worst point of the ellipsoid in the direction \(a_i\) is the center term plus the length of \(B a_i\). That sum has to fit under the bound.

Among the ellipsoids that fit, the largest maximizes \(\log\det B\). That logarithm is concave on positive definite matrices, and each containment inequality describes a convex set of pairs \((B,\ d)\). Maximizing a concave function over a convex set is a convex problem. A singular \(B\) flattens the disk and drops the determinant to zero.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The ellipsoid and the containment test are
\[
\mathcal{E} = \{B u + d : \lVert u\rVert \le 1\},
\]
\[
\lVert B a_i\rVert + a_i^T d \le b_i \quad\text{for every face } i.
\]
\(B\) is symmetric positive definite. The volume objective is \(\log\det B\). On a positive diagonal matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries, so two diagonal shapes with the same product have the same volume factor.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(B = \mathrm{diag}(7,\ 3)\), the center at the origin, and the normal \((1,\ 0)\). The product \(B a\) is \((7,\ 0)\), the length is \(7\), and the center term is zero.

The anchor length is 7. The second diagonal entry never enters, because the normal has a zero in that slot. The determinant of this \(B\) is the product of the diagonal entries.

The anchor determinant is 21. A diagonal shape with the same product has the same volume factor and, along this normal, a different containment length.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Checking one face and skipping the others leaves the ellipsoid free to poke through the rest of the polytope. Dropping the center term, or dropping the length, tests only half of the sum. Squaring the length is a third slip: the support of the unit disk is the length itself. Treating \(\log\det\) as linear in the entries of \(B\) confuses a product of eigenvalues with a sum. A singular \(B\) is not a full ellipsoid. Its determinant is zero and the set is flat.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The containment inequalities are convex and the volume objective is concave, so the fitting problem is a convex program. A primal-dual interior-point method can solve a convex program of this size. Later skills do not require the fitting problem. The picture of an ellipsoid as the image of the unit disk is the part worth keeping.
